newsitem.title: MONACO: RALLYING-LOIX SURPRISES FAVOURITES TO SEIZE MONTE CARLO LEAD.
newsitem.headline: RALLYING-LOIX SURPRISES FAVOURITES TO SEIZE MONTE CARLO LEAD.

text.p: Promising Belgian Freddy Loix surprised the favourites to seize the lead after Sunday's first timed stage of the season-opening Monte Carlo rally.

The 26-year-old Loix, making his debut in the winter classic in a Toyota Celica, covered two laps of a section of the Monaco Grand Prix circuit in a fastest time of two minutes and five seconds on a rainy day.
Drivers raced in pairs in the 2.8-km timed stage, starting at each end of a course using the lower part of the famed track along the Monaco harbour.
The stage was brought in by the organisers as a gesture of goodwill towards International Automobile Federation (FIA) officials, eager to make rallying as exciting to watch as Formula One.
Loix was two seconds faster than double winnner Carlos Sainz of Spain, who took second place in the provisional standings of the world championship event in his Ford Escort.

Italian Piero Liatti and 1995 world champion Colin McRae of Britain, both driving Subaru Imprezas, shared the third fastest time a further one second back with German Dieter Depping's Ford Escort after the first day's single timed stage.
World champion Tommi Makinen of Finland, in his Mitsubishi Lancer, was six seconds slower than Loix and had to be content with the eighth time.

"I'm delighted but I know that this stage is of little significance," said Loix before heading for Valence where the drivers will set out on Monday for five tricky timed stages in the Ardeche mountains.
Sainz, survived a fright, touching the barriers and scratching the rear left wing of his car on the narrow, rain-soaked circuit.
"It was very slippery," said the Spaniard. "I think it was a good idea to use the circuit, it was fun."

The drivers will come back to the circuit on Wednesday for the last stage of the rally, modified this year to comply with a revolution in rules aimed at making the sport more attractive to the public and the media.
Organisers have been forced to drop the concentration run, which saw the drivers set off from several European cities to gather in Monte Carlo for the start of the race.
The Turini night in the mountains overlooking the gambling capital which traditionally ended the rally has also been scrapped.
"Maybe I should regret the Turini night as it was part of the Monte Carlo mystique," said Loix, who was a road-opener in last year's race, which did not count for the world championship.
"But that's the way it is and you have to accept it," he added. "When I see how difficult the rally is going to be now, I'd prefer not to think about previous years."
